title: Keep off the grass? Cannabis, cognition and addiction

claims.statement: In people who used cannabis frequently, the evidence is insufficient to say whether differences in memory and thinking tests remain after they have stopped for days or weeks, and the question is disputed. Differences were smaller in studies that required longer abstinence: in a meta-analysis of cross-sectional studies of adolescents and young adults (Scott et al., 2018; AMSTAR 2 confidence critically low), the 15 studies that required more than 72 hours without cannabis before testing (928 participants; 7 to 90 days by the first reader's reading of the Table) found an average difference from comparison groups with minimal use of −0.08 standard deviations (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07), against −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22) in the 54 studies that required 72 hours or less or did not say (P = .01). This compares different studies, not the same people before and after stopping; the interval includes both no difference and the overall difference of −0.25; only 14 of the 69 studies reported checking abstinence; and 7 of the 15 longer-abstinence studies come from papers by one research group, and 11 of the 15 had age ranges ending at 20 or younger. A systematic review of 2004-2015 studies (Broyd et al., 2016; critically low) found eighteen studies of people abstinent for more than a day, most often 21 to 35 days and few for longer: some found poorer attention, verbal or working memory or psychomotor speed after 23 to 53 days of abstinence, or poorer executive function in older adults abstinent more than 28 days, while others found no difference from controls, including a prospective study in which adolescents who had stopped did not differ from controls and a cohort in which people who had stopped heavy use for at least 12 months did not differ on any test from people who had not used. It rated persistence as mixed for verbal learning and memory, working memory, attention and planning-type executive functions, called recovery contentious and suggested that verbal learning and memory may recover with prolonged abstinence. A narrative review of the same year (Curran et al., 2016) states that studies converge on no impairment beyond 4–6 weeks, citing two earlier sources, and adds that brain cannabinoid receptor levels return to normal after about 4 weeks of monitored abstinence, which is not a test of memory or thinking. In a New Zealand birth cohort, people with persistent dependence that began in adolescence who used cannabis weekly or less in the year before testing at 38 still had lower IQ than in childhood (17 people, p = .03), but they had used on up to 52 days that year and were not compared with people who never used, so this is not a test of abstinence (Meier et al., 2012). The individual abstinence studies are known here only through the reviews' descriptions, and the reviews share studies. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Scott et al. 2018 (raw-score d against comparison groups): required abstinence more than 72 h −0.08 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies, n = 928, P = .29) against 72 h or less −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22; 54 studies, n = 7,799); chi-square 6.36, P = .01; longer mean reported abstinence went with smaller differences (beta 0.059, P = .04 uncorrected; 28 studies); required abstinence mean 152.7 h (SD 335.2), none or unstated in 22 studies, 1 to 72 h in 32, more than 72 h in 15; monitored in 14. Broyd et al. 2016: eighteen abstinence studies (eleven cross-sectional, abstinent 7 days to more than 1 year; seven prospective, 21 days to 4–8 years); persistence rated +– for verbal learning and memory (9 studies), working memory (7), attention (10), planning-type executive functions (9) and verbal fluency (4), + for psychomotor function (6), – for other memory functions, time estimation and decision making. Meier et al. 2012: adolescent-onset persistent dependence with weekly or less use in the year before testing (median 14 days, range 0 to 52; n = 17), childhood to adult IQ about 102 to 97.5, p = .03 (values read from a figure).

claims.statement: In adolescents and young adults who use cannabis frequently or heavily, compared with people of similar age who use little or no cannabis, cannabis use is associated with slightly lower scores on memory and thinking tests in studies that did not give cannabis to participants (the hours after a single dose given in a laboratory are covered by the answer on how long impairment lasts). In a meta-analysis of 69 cross-sectional samples published 1973 to 2017 (2,152 people who used cannabis, mean age 20.6, and 6,575 comparison participants with minimal use; Scott et al., 2018; AMSTAR 2 confidence critically low), the average difference in raw test scores, not adjusted for other drug use, education or ability before use, was about a quarter of a standard deviation (d −0.25, 95% CI −0.32 to −0.17): learning −0.33, executive shifting −0.30, delayed memory −0.26, speed of processing −0.26, inhibition −0.25, working memory −0.22 and attention −0.21, with no clear difference on visuospatial (−0.04, −0.16 to 0.08) or motor tests (−0.02, −0.22 to 0.18). Results varied widely between studies (editors' approximate 95% prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); 22 of the 69 studies required no abstinence before testing or did not say; samples of people seeking treatment differed more (−0.43, −0.62 to −0.24; 12 studies); and small studies reported larger differences: allowing for missing small studies shrank the estimate of a simpler model from −0.21 to −0.13. The difference depended on how recently people had used: it was −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies) in studies that required more than 72 hours without cannabis before testing, against −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22) in studies that required 72 hours or less or did not say, a comparison between studies rather than within the same people (see the answer on stopping). A systematic review of 2004-2015 studies (Broyd et al., 2016; critically low; nothing pooled) rated the evidence of poorer verbal learning and memory and attention in people who use cannabis regularly as strong and largely consistent (20 and 14 studies), and the evidence for working memory, planning-type executive functions, inhibition and decision making as mixed; more than half of its studies did not report IQ or education, and its authors suggest that links with how often people use may reflect lingering effects of recent use. Two cohorts that measured IQ in childhood add to this: in a British twin cohort, the 84 of 1,989 18-year-olds with cannabis dependence scored lower than the others on 4 of 6 executive-function scores, 2 after allowing for IQ at 12, but did not differ from their co-twins in 57 pairs in which only one twin was dependent (Meier et al., 2018); in a New Zealand birth cohort, scores at 38 on 9 of 16 memory, speed and executive tests were lower the more often people had met criteria for dependence at five interviews from 18 to 38, after allowing for childhood IQ and sex, though these tests had not been given in childhood (Meier et al., 2012). The two reviews share primary studies and are counted once. None of these comparisons can show that cannabis caused the differences. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Scott et al. 2018 (69 samples; 2,152 against 6,575; raw-score Hedges-corrected d, negative = lower in the cannabis groups): overall −0.247 (95% CI −0.32 to −0.17), between-study variance 0.070 (P < .001; editors' approximate prediction interval −0.77 to +0.28); learning −0.33 (−0.42 to −0.24); executive abstraction/shifting −0.30 (−0.40 to −0.20); speed −0.26 (−0.38 to −0.15); delayed memory −0.26 (−0.35 to −0.16); inhibition −0.25 (−0.38 to −0.13); updating/working memory −0.22 (−0.31 to −0.12); attention −0.21 (−0.31 to −0.12); verbal/language −0.14 (−0.27 to 0.001); visuospatial −0.04 (−0.16 to 0.08); motor −0.02 (−0.22 to 0.18). Required abstinence more than 72 h −0.08 (−0.22 to 0.07; 15 studies, n = 928) against 72 h or less −0.30 (−0.37 to −0.22; 54 studies, n = 7,799), P = .01. Treatment-seeking −0.43 (−0.62 to −0.24; 12 studies) against others −0.22 (−0.29 to −0.14), uncorrected P = .04. Small-study effects: Egger t = 4.70, P < .001; trim-and-fill in a univariate model −0.206 to −0.128. Broyd et al. 2016 (qualitative ratings, chronic use): verbal learning and memory +++ (20 studies), attention +++ (14), working memory +– (16), planning-type executive functions +– (23), inhibition +– (9), decision making +– (17), psychomotor function + (10). Meier et al. 2018 (age 18; 84 with dependence among 1,989; sex-adjusted z-scores): 4 of 6 executive scores lower (Spatial Span Forward −0.48 against 0.02), 2 of 6 after IQ at 12; 57 discordant twin pairs, no significant difference (Spatial Span Forward −0.38 against −0.18, p = .20). Meier et al. 2012 (age 38; tests without childhood baseline, adjusted for childhood IQ and sex): significant trend with waves of dependence on 9 of 16 tests.

claims.statement: In people who use cannabis, using it more often and starting younger are associated with a higher share meeting criteria for dependence in the figures that narrative reviews cite, but most of these figures are second-hand and rest on different designs and definitions, and in the one national survey analysis read that adjusted for other disorders, starting early went with a lower, not a higher, hazard of dependence. By frequency of use (second-hand): 17.0% of people who smoked cannabis weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021, which also calls this almost 1 in 19, although 9.7% is about 1 in 10); 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by Connor et al., 2021) or up to one-third of people who use daily (a UN report cited by the same review); half of people who use daily, from a 3-year prospective study of frequent use (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015); and 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily, cited to a review that does not contain the figure (Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), so it cannot be traced. No definitions or adjustment are given with these figures. By age of first use (second-hand): one in six of people who start in adolescence, against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, citing a 2006 book chapter; Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, with 17% in its table); people who start in adolescence about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014); and first use before 16 linked to a higher risk and faster progression (Connor et al., 2021, citing three sources). In the 1990-92 US National Comorbidity Survey, by age at interview rather than age at first use, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of people aged 15 to 24 who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), against 8.1% at 25 to 34, 8.5% at 35 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years in which to become dependent; the authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). In the 2001-05 US NESARC (7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence; recalled ages), first use before 14, compared with first use at 14 or later, went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47) and a lower one after stepwise adjustment for sociodemographic factors, psychiatric disorders and dependence on other substances (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors read early onset as a marker of other psychiatric and substance use problems rather than a risk factor in itself (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). In a 3-year prospective study of people who used frequently, measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016), and twin studies find shared genetic and environmental influences on starting early (Connor et al., 2021). None of the sources measured how much THC people took, and, in the editors' reading, frequent use is partly built into what dependence means (its criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using), so the two are hard to separate. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Second-hand frequency figures: 17.0% weekly and 19.0% daily meeting dependence criteria; 9.7% of weekly smokers without dependence dependent within a year (Cougle 2016 via Connor 2021); 30-40% with a history of daily use (two reviews via Connor 2021); up to one-third of people using daily (UN report via Connor 2021); half of people using daily (van der Pol 2013 via Hall 2015); 25-50% of daily smokers (Volkow 2014, not traceable). Second-hand age figures: one in six with adolescent onset (book chapter via Hall 2009 and Hall 2015; 17% in Volkow 2014 Table 1); 2-4 times dependence symptoms within 2 years, adolescent against adult onset (Chen 2009 via Volkow 2014). NCS 1990-92 by age at interview, DSM-III-R dependence among people who had used: 15-24, 15.3% (SE 2.3); 25-34, 8.1% (0.7); 35-44, 8.5% (1.3); 45-54, 3.1% (1.5). NESARC 2001-05, first use before 14: unadjusted HR 2.47; adjusted 0.63 (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9); in the adjusted model mood disorder 2.69, personality disorder 2.30, anxiety disorder 2.31, cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3 to 7.6), alcohol dependence 2.55.

claims.statement: In US national household surveys, about 9 in 100 people who had ever used cannabis had at some point met criteria for cannabis dependence under older, narrower diagnostic definitions. In the National Comorbidity Survey (fieldwork 1990 to 1992; a probability sample of 8,098 people aged 15 to 54; response 82.4%; a standardized interview, the CIDI, given by lay interviewers), 46.3% of the population had ever used cannabis and 4.2% had ever met DSM-III-R criteria for cannabis dependence, so 9.1% (SE 0.7; about 7.7% to 10.5%, editors' calculation) of the people who had ever used it, even once, had ever been dependent by the time of the interview, against 31.9% for tobacco, 23.1% for heroin, 16.7% for cocaine and 15.4% for alcohol in the same survey; among people who had used cannabis, 12.0% of men and 5.5% of women had been dependent (Anthony et al., 1994). The dependence questions were asked only of people who reported at least several occasions of use, people who had started recently had had little time to become dependent, and the authors expect incomplete reporting, and the survey's leaving out people who had died, to lower the figures, while casual use that people forget or do not mention would push them the other way. In the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions (interviews in 2001 to 2002 and 2004 to 2005; 7,389 adults who had ever used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence by a structured interview, the AUDADIS-IV), a survival analysis of recalled ages of first use and of onset estimated that 8.9% of people who used cannabis would become dependent at some time in their life (no interval given), 5.9% within 10 years of first use and about 2% within the first year, with a median of about 5 years from first use to dependence; the corresponding lifetime figures were 67.5% for nicotine, 22.7% for alcohol and 20.9% for cocaine (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). The figure of about 9 in 100, or about 1 in 10, that narrative reviews repeat is cited to these surveys or matches them (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, cite a 2006 book chapter for it, with their comparison figures from the 1990-92 survey; Volkow et al., 2014, and Curran et al., 2016, cite the 2001-05 analysis; Connor et al., 2021, the 1990-92 survey); the reviews' figures are second-hand. DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence are narrower than DSM-5 cannabis use disorder, which needs 2 of 11 criteria within 12 months and includes mild cases (Connor et al., 2021). That review cites about 30% of people who use cannabis as developing a use disorder in more recent US national data, without giving the measure (Hasin et al., 2015, not read here), and the pooled figures of a 2020 meta-analysis of general-population studies are given in the claim on cannabis strength and dependence. Both surveys are from the US, leave out people living in institutions, rely on what people recalled and reported, and predate legal markets and today's stronger products; figures by how often people use and by the age at which they started are in the claim on frequency and age of starting. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: NCS 1990-92 (weighted, n = 8,098; Table 2): cannabis lifetime use 46.3% (SE 1.1), lifetime dependence 4.2% (0.3), dependence among people who had used 9.1% (0.7; editors' 95% CI about 7.7% to 10.5%); tobacco 31.9% (no SE), heroin 23.1% (5.6), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), alcohol 15.4% (0.7); among people who had used cannabis, men 12.0% (1.1), women 5.5% (0.7) (Table 5). NESARC 2001-05 (7,389 who had used cannabis; actuarial survival estimates, no intervals): lifetime cumulative probability of DSM-IV dependence 8.9% (nicotine 67.5%, alcohol 22.7%, cocaine 20.9%); 5.9% within 10 years of first use; about 2% within the first year; median time from first use to dependence about 5 years. Second-hand: about 30% developing a use disorder in more recent US data, measure not given (Connor et al., 2021, citing Hasin et al., 2015).

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether using cannabis as a teenager lowers IQ later in life, and the question is disputed. In a New Zealand birth cohort (Dunedin; 874 people analysed, born 1972-73; full-scale IQ tested at 7 to 13, when only 7 of 1,037 cohort members had tried cannabis, and again at 38; Meier et al., 2012), IQ rose by 0.05 standard deviations in the 242 people who never used cannabis (99.84 to 100.64) and fell by 0.38 (99.68 to 93.93, about 6 points) in the 38 people (about 4 in 100 of those analysed, editors' arithmetic; 82% men) who met criteria for cannabis dependence at 3 or more of 5 interviews between 18 and 38, with intermediate changes in between (linear trend t = −4.45, adjusted for sex). The trend held when people who had used cannabis in the day or week before testing, or had persistent tobacco, alcohol or hard-drug dependence or schizophrenia, were left out in turn, and after adjustment for education (t = −3.41), but its test statistic about halved (t = −2.20) when recent use, other dependence and schizophrenia were adjusted together, and no adjusted size or interval is reported. The decline was larger when dependence began before 18 (about −0.54 against −0.14 standard deviations at 3 or more interviews; 23 and 14 people), with no test of the difference; the 8 points that some reviews quote refer to these 23 people. A simulation by another researcher showed that differences in family socioeconomic status could produce the main pattern with no effect of cannabis (Rogeberg, 2013); in reply, the original team reported that family socioeconomic status did not predict adolescent-onset dependence or IQ change, and that the trend coefficient barely changed when socioeconomic status or childhood self-control was added, each on its own, or when only the 553 people from middle-class families were analysed (−0.152, then −0.158, −0.151 and −0.155; Moffitt et al., 2013). Two US twin cohorts with lighter, shorter use (ever use by 17 to 20 against never; 789 and 2,277 twins; subtests at 9 to 12 and again at 17 to 20) found that those who used fell 4.0 and 3.4 points further behind age peers on Vocabulary, adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, socioeconomic status and cohort, but not on four other subtests; in the larger cohort lower scores preceded use and the Vocabulary difference shrank to −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6) after adjustment for drinking and other drug use (in the other it stayed at −3.7); and the twin who used did not differ significantly from the co-twin who did not (identical pairs −5.4, −11.2 to 0.5, 25 pairs; −0.7, −3.9 to 2.4, 112 pairs), with intervals wide enough to include the between-family differences (Jackson et al., 2016). In a British twin cohort (1,989 people tested at 5, 12 and 18), the 84 with cannabis dependence at 18 already had lower IQ at 5 and 12 (by 5.23 and 5.61 points, sex-adjusted), their IQ did not fall significantly more between 12 and 18 (−1.73 points, p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 0.9), and in 57 twin pairs in which only one twin was dependent, the twins did not differ at any age (Meier et al., 2018). The three Dunedin papers concern one cohort and count once; the twin cohorts studied mostly light use in late adolescence, while Dunedin studied dependence persisting into midlife. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Dunedin (Meier et al. 2012; sex-adjusted; IQ change in SD units, IQ points divided by 15): never used +0.05 (n = 242); used, never dependent −0.07 (479); dependence at 1 wave −0.11 (80), 2 waves −0.17 (35), 3 or more −0.38 (38; 99.68 to 93.93); trend t = −4.45, P < 0.0001; education-adjusted t = −3.41; multivariable t = −2.20, P = 0.0282; no coefficients or intervals reported. Onset before against after 18 at 3 or more waves about −0.54 (n = 23) against −0.14 (n = 14), p = .02 (read from a figure). Moffitt et al. 2013 (same cohort): β −0.152 (sex only), −0.158 (plus socioeconomic status), −0.151 (plus childhood self-control), −0.155 (553 from middle-class families); socioeconomic status and adolescent-onset dependence χ2 = 1.15, P = 0.56; socioeconomic status and IQ change r = −0.006. Rogeberg 2013: simulation with no effect of cannabis, trend test significant at 5% in about 50% of 500 runs. Jackson et al. 2016 (ever use against never; IQ points; adjusted for age, sex, race, zygosity, socioeconomic status and cohort): Vocabulary −4.0 (−6.3 to −1.7; RFAB) and −3.4 (−4.5 to −2.3; MTFS); with drinking and other drugs −3.7 (−6.8 to −0.5) and −0.8 (−2.3 to 0.6); co-twin Vocabulary, identical pairs −5.4 (−11.2 to 0.5; 25 pairs) and −0.7 (−3.9 to 2.4; 112 pairs), non-identical −2.8 (−7.7 to 2.2; 54) and 0.2 (−2.8 to 3.3; 99); 47 pairs discordant for heavy use −1.5 (−5.5 to 2.6). Meier et al. 2018 (dependence at 18, 84 against 1,905; sex-adjusted IQ points): age 5 −5.23, age 12 −5.61, age 18 −7.34; change 12 to 18 −1.73 (p = .20; editors' approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 0.9); 57 discordant pairs, age 18 −1.45 (p = .42; approximately −5.0 to 2.1), change 0.05 (p = .98); frequency, change beta −0.05 (p = .035) in the full sample and −0.02 (p = .46) within pairs.

claims.statement: In observational samples of people who used cannabis regularly or had a cannabis use disorder, the share with cannabis withdrawal, as each study defined it, depended strongly on where the sample came from, in a 2020 meta-analysis of 50 cohorts with 23,518 participants (searched to June 2019; Bahji et al., 2020; AMSTAR 2 critically low; English only; no group of people who did not cut down for comparison): 17 in 100 (95% CI 13 to 22) in 15 general-population samples holding 17,475 people, 54 in 100 (48 to 59) in 28 outpatient samples (5,684 people) and 87 in 100 (79 to 94) in 7 inpatient or residential samples (357 people). Withdrawal at any time in life was reported far more often than withdrawal in the past year (76 in 100, 70 to 82, in 18 cohorts, against 31 in 100, 27 to 36, in 32), and the one general-population sample assessed with DSM-5 criteria found it in 12.1% of 1,527 people. The review's headline figure, 47 in 100 (41 to 52; I2 99.2%; cohorts from 8% to 100%), is close to the plain average of the cohort estimates and is driven by small clinical samples; the review's own count, 6,469 of 23,518 participants, is about 27.5 in 100 (editors' calculation on the study card). Men and women did not differ (27 and 26 in 100, 15 studies), although the review's conclusions say withdrawal was more common in men. In DSM-5, cannabis withdrawal means at least three of seven symptoms within about a week of stopping or cutting down: irritability, anger or aggression; nervousness or anxiety; sleep difficulty; less appetite or weight loss; restlessness; low mood; and physical symptoms such as headache, sweating or stomach pain (as summarised by Bahji et al., 2020, and Connor et al., 2021). As described in narrative reviews, whose figures are second-hand, symptoms typically begin 1 to 2 days after stopping, peak within the first week (at 2 to 6 days in one account) and fade within 1 to 2 weeks (Curran et al., 2016; Connor et al., 2021); craving, nightmares and nausea are also prominent, and THC relieves the symptoms in a dose-dependent way (Curran et al., 2016); people seeking help to stop most often report anxiety, sleep problems, appetite disturbance and low mood (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), often severe enough to impair everyday life (Hall, 2015); one review gives around half of people who use daily as having withdrawal when they stop, citing an earlier review (Curran et al., 2016); and in people without other medical or psychiatric illness withdrawal is described as carrying no serious risk and usually needing only supportive care (Connor et al., 2021). Sleep after stopping is covered in more detail in the claims on sleep. The cohorts defined regular use differently, most predate DSM-5, the review took the lowest threshold where studies offered several, cohorts with more tobacco use reported more withdrawal (a comparison between studies), and in people who use both daily, stopping both gives stronger symptoms than stopping either alone (Curran et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Bahji 2020, random-effects pooled prevalence: general population 17% (95% CI 13 to 22; 15 cohorts; 17,475 people; I2 98%); outpatient 54% (48 to 59; 28; 5,684); inpatient 87% (79 to 94; 7; 357); past year 31% (27 to 36; 32 cohorts); lifetime 76% (70 to 82; 18); overall 47% (41 to 52; 50 cohorts; I2 99.2%; range 8% to 100%); men 27% (21 to 34), women 26% (19 to 33), P = .99; one DSM-5 population cohort 12.1% of 1,527. Editors' calculation on the card: 6,470 of 23,518 participants (27.5%). Time course as described in reviews: onset 1-2 days (24-48 hours), peak within the first week (2-6 days), resolution within 1-2 weeks.
